claims.text: Replacing conventional high-thermal-load additive manufacturing with binder jetting followed by controlled isothermal sintering will reduce residual thermal stresses in AlCrFeNiSi miniature components.
Binder jetting followed by controlled isothermal sintering will improve the mechanical properties of AlCrFeNiSi miniature components.
A non-beam process can form a green body that is subsequently consolidated through interdiffusion and sintering.
Sintering below the AlCrFeNiSi melting point will promote full interdiffusion.
An 800–900 °C sintering window will provide sufficient diffusion in AlCrFeNiSi.
Sintering AlCrFeNiSi at 800–900 °C will avoid excessive grain growth.
Sintering AlCrFeNiSi at 800–900 °C will avoid undesired phase changes.
The proposed route is applicable to miniature features ranging from approximately 100 µm to a few millimeters.
Binder jetting and isothermal sintering will produce a more homogeneous AlCrFeNiSi microstructure.
The resulting microstructure will contain equiaxed grains.
The resulting microstructure will contain fewer residual dislocations.
Avoiding rapid localized melting and solidification will minimize thermal shock and steep temperature gradients.
Uniform isothermal sintering enables gradual interdiffusion and consolidation.
Gradual interdiffusion and consolidation will alleviate internal stresses.
Binder-jetted and sintered components will have greater tensile strength than components made by high-thermal-load additive manufacturing.
Binder-jetted and sintered components will have greater ductility than components made by high-thermal-load additive manufacturing.
Binder jetting and sintering will provide simpler process control than high-thermal-load additive manufacturing.
Binder-jetted and sintered components will contain fewer defects than components made by high-thermal-load additive manufacturing.
Conventional laser powder-bed fusion is known to cause significant residual stress, degraded mechanical properties, and processing complexity specifically in AlCrFeNiSi components.
Using dimensions or sintering conditions outside the proposed range may cause incomplete densification or microstructural inhomogeneity.
